Conditions that are not currently managed with pharmacotherapy may be unintentionally omitted by patients, particularly older individuals who may not appreciate their relevance to dental care. Conversely, clinicians may focus heavily on medication-related risks, such as bisphosphonate use, while the underlying disease itself remains undisclosed.

The case also prompted reflection on the potential value of greater integration between primary dental care and wider NHS medical records. With appropriate patient consent, access for general dental practitioners to elements of the NHS National Care Records Service, formerly known as the Summary Care Record, could support safer decision-making for older or medically complex patients.4 Such access would not replace careful history taking or clinical judgement but could provide a valuable safety net where important information is inadvertently omitted.

General dental practitioners routinely undertake invasive procedures in primary care settings. Ensuring that treatment

planning is informed by a complete understanding of patients’ medical background is therefore essential.5 Alongside thorough and probing history taking, improved digital integration between dentistry and the wider NHS may represent a crucial step toward enhancing patient safety.

# Dentistry in the dark

I wish to share a recent clinical encounter that reinforced, for me as a foundation dentist, both the importance of careful medical history taking and the limitations of relying solely on patient-reported information.

An 87-year-old patient attended with their daughter for a new patient examination. The patient brought a detailed list of repeat prescriptions and reported no medical conditions beyond those suggested by her medication list. Based on this information, I formulated a treatment plan that included dental extractions. However, later in the appointment the patient mentioned, almost in passing, that they had Paget’s disease and had previously received treatment at a specialist centre, though the patient could not recall the details. This diagnosis had not emerged during the initial medical history discussion, and its disclosure prompted reconsideration of my risk assessment prior to undertaking extractions.

Paget’s disease is characterised by abnormal bone remodelling that produces structurally disorganised bone which may be enlarged, hypervascular and mechanically weaker.1 In the context of dental extractions, this can present practical challenges including increased surgical difficulty, delayed healing and susceptibility to infection.2 Osteonecrosis of the jaw is most strongly associated with antiresorptive therapy such as bisphosphonates; however, underlying metabolic bone disease may still influence surgical risk and healing outcomes.3 Had this diagnosis not surfaced prior to treatment, the patient may have been exposed to avoidable complications.
